title: Games beyond Games

outline.subsection: Chapter opening (unnamed) — three traditional axes + chapter roadmap
outline.summary: Calleja names the three principal analytic axes along which game research distributes itself — formal (game as media object), experiential (player gameplay), sociocultural (gaming communities) — and explicitly positions the present book on the experiential axis while affirming that the other two will continue to inform the analysis. Announces a chapter agenda: clarify the family of games at issue + describe their constituent elements so that later vocabulary (players, rules, environmental properties) carries determinate sense.

Argues that games elude holistic categorization and that stable universal definitions inevitably under-cover the phenomenon. The performance of a game inhabits two often-simultaneous domains — the player's subjective experience and the visible practice of play — and a game only becomes a game in being played; until then it is only rules + props awaiting human engagement. Human subjectivity is therefore at the heart of analytic difficulty. The term 'game' subsumes radically disparate activities (poker, fencing, Grand Theft Auto IV), and digital games heighten the complexity (GTA IV is better described as a virtual environment containing several embedded games + a linear storyline).

Adopts Wittgenstein's family-resemblance proposal: games are not a rigidly defined set but a family whose members overlap in resemblances. Analytic boundaries are admitted as legitimate but artificial; subset-claims need not identify games as a whole. The rationale is operational, not merely philosophical: family-resemblance specificity wards off Arne Naess's 'verbal disagreement' — disputes over claims whose disputants are tacitly invoking different exemplars (e.g. Tetris vs. Half-Life 2). The chapter's remaining task is therefore to deliver a descriptive framework that identifies the matrix of components combining to form games and virtual environments.

Distinguishes game-as-object from game-as-process. Settlers of Catan exemplifies the dual aspect: the material set of pieces + rules vs. the situated activity afforded by them. The object/process distinction carries over to digital games — rules coded into software, material substrate being hardware + code — yet preserves the asymmetry: the dormant code, board pieces, or rule set present a potential that is actualized during gameplay. Calleja then pivots to the processual perspective endorsed by T. L. Taylor (2006) and Thomas Malaby (2007), citing Malaby's claim that each game is an ongoing process that always contains the potential for generating new practices and meanings, possibly refiguring the game itself. The processual framing implies games are not experientially separate from other domains of experience — a direct anticipatory pushback against Suits's 'lusory attitude' as taken up by Salen+Zimmerman (2003) and Juul (2005), flagged for full treatment in Ch.3.

Rather than an essentialist definition (as in Juul 2005 or Salen+Zimmerman 2003), the book adopts Wittgenstein's family approach and narrows focus to a subset of the game family found within virtual environments. Names five constituent elements that interact to express different configurations of games + virtual environments: (1) human player, (2) representational sign, (3) structural properties of game and environment (split below into coded rules + simulated environmental properties), (4) material medium. The next five subsections describe each in turn.

'Player' designates the human agent(s) engaging with the game system — used in conformity with game-studies convention, NOT to prescribe an experiential disposition (e.g. 'playfulness'). The object/process split returns: from the object-side the player is the ideal/implied player; from the process-side the player is the actual active agent + the set of practices she deploys, always considered relative to her social/cultural context (which has a formative role in disposition prior to and during engagement). Calleja then notes a key processual corollary: different players engaging the same structure/signs/medium can experience a different game — illustrated with a Call of Duty IV death-match where one player follows team-kill conventions while a teammate pursues an idiosyncratic suicide-jump goal.

The representational sign denotes the broader category of signifying entity — alphanumeric text, imagery, or sound — i.e. the interpretable surface elements players read to interact with the game. In digital games the representational sign and the executable behaviour-code may both be 'code' but are functionally distinct and worth separating for analytic purposes.

Imports Espen Aarseth's (1997) Cybertext: in ergodic media the 'surface sign' bears a nontrivial relation to the mechanical operations of the internal code that generates it — they are mutually intrinsic, unlike trivial cases (a literary text read aloud is a derivative of the printed book). Calleja then notes that rules are a common denominator across the game family but their shape varies — analog rules are stipulated by the game but enforced/modified socially; digital rules are coded into software and harder to amend. Multiplayer digital games typically display a coexistence of coded and socially-negotiated rules — paradigm: a Counter-Strike: Source clan permitting the standard ruleset but locally banning sniper rifles + enforcing the ban through warnings and server-bans.

Simulated environmental properties obtain whenever a game takes place in a constructed environment that models physical properties — not restricted to computer-generated environments, since tabletop RPGs also simulate physics through game-system rules (the 3D6-damage-from-three-meter-fall example). In computer-generated environments the physics is hard-coded (Call of Duty IV brick density and bullet penetration; avatar movement speeds), and these details feed back into the rules of the game and the balance/enjoyability of experience. The contrast with analog: in the analog case the environmental mechanics are upheld by players according to a prescribed (often modified) system, whereas in the digital case they are upheld by the computer. Complexity ranges from minimal (Pong) to fuller-but-always-partial simulation (Crysis, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2).

The material instantiation of the game shapes its form + experience: PS3-vs-PC inflects a real-time-strategy title (controller vs. mouse); Nintendo DS handhelds permit pocket-portable + infrared-linked social contexts that home PCs do not. The contrast is starkest for board-games-in-code: even when the rules of Settlers of Catan are preserved in software, the absence of physical board / cards / pieces produces a markedly different incarnation of Settlers — and whether to call it a different game altogether is less important than having an analytical instrument that can register the difference.

Synthesis: a considerable proportion of what are called digital games today are in fact extended virtual environments that contain a game or multiple games within them. Apply the five-element framework to Grand Theft Auto IV and one sees several clusters of game-rules co-present in one overall environment; the material medium / signs / environmental properties remain constant across the embedded games, but the conventional + coded rules + player-aspects vary. In Wittgensteinian terms, GTA IV, World of Warcraft, and Half-Life 2 belong to two families that mingle resemblances (games + virtual environments) and form a sub-family derived from both. Ryan (2006) is cited approvingly: digital games and tabletop RPGs combine traditional games' rule-systems with the fictional / narrative resources of their predecessor media. To denominate this hybrid sub-family the book introduces 'virtual game environments' (or 'game environments') — the intersection of the game-family and the virtual-environment-family, which becomes the volume's unit of analysis. Digitized card games (hearts, poker) and puzzle games (crosswords, sudoku) are excluded; focus is on games that present a virtual world for participation (Half-Life 2, World of Warcraft).

concepts.label: three traditional analytic axes of game research (formal / experiential / sociocultural)
concepts.summary: Calleja's tripartite mapping of how game research is broadly distributed: formal (game-as-media-object), experiential (player-gameplay-subjectivity), sociocultural (gaming communities). The book is positioned on the experiential axis but admits formal + sociocultural insights as informants.

concepts.label: experiential-axis self-positioning of the volume
concepts.summary: Explicit positioning move — declares the book's primary analytic commitment as experiential; presupposed by the entire PIM apparatus to follow.

concepts.label: family-resemblance definition of games (via Wittgenstein 1997)
concepts.summary: The book's methodological commitment: games are not a rigidly-defined set but a family whose members share overlapping resemblances; analytic boundaries are admitted as artificial. This is Calleja's first and most consequential methodological move — it returns at p.11 (against essentialist definitions) and at p.14 (digital games as hybrid sub-family of two families). Foreshadows the family-resemblance logic that re-emerges as PIM-dimensions-as-overlapping-non-essential-axes (IG-03) and incorporation-as-family-resemblance-of-experiential-modes (IG-10).

concepts.label: verbal disagreement (via Arne Naess 2005)
concepts.summary: Methodological hazard whereby disputants make incompatible claims because they tacitly invoke different exemplars (Tetris vs. Half-Life 2). Family-resemblance specificity is Calleja's prophylactic; the worry will recur in Ch.2 (immersion debates) and Ch.3 (lusory-attitude critique).

concepts.label: game-as-object vs. game-as-process distinction
concepts.summary: The dormant code, board pieces, or rule set present a potential that is actualized during gameplay. Applied to digital + analog games alike. Provides the conceptual scaffolding for processual game-ontology and prefigures the macro/micro temporal-phase distinction of IG-03 (a game's macro-phase is closer to object-side anticipations of process; its micro-phase IS the process).

concepts.label: processual approach to games (via T. L. Taylor 2006 + Malaby 2007)
concepts.summary: Calleja endorses Malaby's claim that each game is an ongoing process that always contains potential for generating new practices and meanings, possibly refiguring the game itself. Processuality entails continuity with other domains of experience and refuses the experiential-separateness implied by 'lusory attitude' (Suits 1978 via Salen+Zimmerman 2003 + Juul 2005).

concepts.label: lusory attitude (Suits 1978 — prospective for Ch.3 full treatment)
concepts.summary: Cited prospectively only; full critical treatment deferred to Ch.3. Here invoked as the foil against which the processual continuity-with-experience claim is mobilized.

concepts.label: five-element descriptive framework (player / representational sign / coded rules / [simulated] environmental properties / material medium)
concepts.summary: Calleja's load-bearing descriptive decomposition introduced as the analytic instrument BEFORE the PIM proper. The framework is non-essentialist (consistent with family-resemblance) — it identifies a matrix of components that interact to express different configurations of games + virtual environments, not necessary-and-sufficient conditions. Two of the elements (coded rules + simulated environmental properties) are clustered in the chapter's header at p.11 under 'structural properties of game and environment' and broken out in subsequent subsections.

concepts.label: the player (element 1) — human agent, NOT 'playfulness-bearer'
concepts.summary: Calleja stipulates that 'player' designates the human agent engaging with the system, not a particular experiential disposition. Object-side: implied/ideal player. Process-side: active player + practices, always indexed to social/cultural context. The Call of Duty IV death-match example demonstrates that same object + different practices = different game-process.

concepts.label: the representational sign (element 2)
concepts.summary: The interpretable, representational entity (text/image/sound) that players read to interact with the game. In digital games the representational sign and the behaviour-generating code may both be code but perform functionally distinct roles — separation is analytic, not ontological.

concepts.label: coded rules (element 3a) + coded/socially-negotiated rule coexistence
concepts.summary: In analog games rules are stipulated by the game but enforced socially; in digital games rules are coded into software and harder to amend; multiplayer digital games typically combine coded with socially-negotiated rules. The Counter-Strike: Source sniper-ban-by-clan example demonstrates the negotiated layer riding atop the coded layer.

concepts.label: ergodic vs. non-ergodic media + nontrivial code-to-surface-sign relation (Aarseth 1997)
concepts.summary: Aarseth's distinction between trivial textual derivation (literary text read aloud) and nontrivial cybernetic-sign production (code + interpretable surface are mutually intrinsic). Recurs in IG-03 as ergodicity-as-dispositional-readiness.

concepts.label: (simulated) environmental properties (element 3b) — computer-upheld vs. player-upheld
concepts.summary: Properties that model physical characteristics of a constructed environment. Computer-generated: hard-coded (CoD IV bullet penetration, avatar movement). Analog: maintained by players per a prescribed system (tabletop RPG 3D6-damage). Complexity ranges from minimal abstraction (Pong) to fuller-but-always-partial simulation (Crysis, CoD: MW2).

concepts.label: material medium (element 4) — platform shapes experience
concepts.summary: Hardware specificity inflects the game's form + experience: PS3 vs. PC for an RTS title; Nintendo DS portability/infrared enabling distinctive social contexts; Settlers of Catan board-vs-software variants — even with identical rules, the absence of physical pieces yields a markedly different incarnation. Calleja deflects the question of whether such variants are 'the same game' in favor of the question of whether the analytic instrument can register the difference.

concepts.label: virtual game environments (the volume's unit of analysis)
concepts.summary: The hybrid sub-family at the intersection of games-family and virtual-environments-family. Excludes digitized card/puzzle games (hearts, poker, crosswords, sudoku) and includes games that present a virtual world for participation (Half-Life 2, WoW). This unit-of-analysis declaration is FOUNDATIONAL: every subsequent dimension chapter operates within this scope.

concepts.label: digital games as hybrids of two Wittgensteinian families
concepts.summary: The most distinctive synthesis of the chapter: contemporary digital games like GTA IV, WoW, Half-Life 2 belong simultaneously to the game-family and the virtual-environment-family — they form a sub-family derived from both via mingled resemblances. Justifies why game-definitions that try to span board games + digital games tend to struggle: they treat one family as primary. Ryan (2006) cited as corroborating witness — digital games + tabletop RPGs combine rule-system + narrative/fictional resources.

concepts.label: principled refusal of essentialist definition of games
concepts.summary: The volume's first explicit POSITION-edge: rather than essentialist definitions (e.g. Juul 2005 and Salen+Zimmerman 2003), Calleja follows Wittgenstein in viewing games as members of an extended family that share resemblances. This is the methodological seed-claim that authorizes (i) the five-element descriptive framework and (ii) the family-resemblance logic that returns as PIM-dimensions (IG-03) and incorporation-as-family-resemblance-of-experience (IG-10). PROPAGATED FINDING from IG-03 + IG-10: Calleja's family-resemblance methodology is iteratively applied — at the level of game-definition (IG-01), involvement-decomposition (IG-03), and experiential synthesis (IG-10). Family-resemblance is not a local move but the volume's METHODOLOGICAL SIGNATURE.

concepts.label: games as recursive process of exploration into collective knowledge + social practices
concepts.summary: Auxiliary claim: games reflect aspects of the society/culture that made them while contributing to that society in the process — understanding games is therefore a recursive process. Foreshadows the social/sociocultural-axis import despite the volume's experiential commitment.

concepts.label: dual-domain performance of a game (subjective experience + visible practice)
concepts.summary: Argues that gameplay is performed in two often-simultaneous domains — the player's subjective experience and the visible practice of playing. Anticipates the macro/micro temporal-phase distinction of IG-03 and bears (uncited) phenomenological resonance with Husserlian inner-outer-time-consciousness and Heideggerian Befindlichkeit+verstehen.

positions.label: Calleja vs. Juul (2005) Half-Real on essentialist game-definition
positions.thesis: Rather than adhering to an essentialist definition of games like Juul's classical-game-model, the book follows Wittgenstein in viewing games as members of an extended family that share resemblances.

positions.label: Calleja vs. Salen + Zimmerman (2003) Rules of Play on essentialist game-definition
positions.thesis: The Salen+Zimmerman synthetic essentialist definition is refused for the same reason as Juul's: family-resemblance + the five-element framework supplant necessary-and-sufficient conditions.

positions.label: Calleja endorses processual approach (Taylor 2006 + Malaby 2007)
positions.thesis: Taylor's and Malaby's processual view of games is endorsed against the over-emphasis on game-as-object in earlier prominent texts; each game is an ongoing process that contains potential for generating new practices and meanings.

positions.label: Volume's experiential-axis commitment with non-exclusion of formal + sociocultural
positions.thesis: The book focuses chiefly on the experiential aspects of games, but the formal and sociocultural axes necessarily inform the exploration of player involvement.

positions.label: Virtual game environments as the volume's unit of analysis (exclusion of card/puzzle digital games)
positions.thesis: The book will focus on virtual game environments — the intersection of the game-family and the virtual-environment-family — and will not consider at length digitized hearts/poker/crosswords/sudoku. Half-Life 2 and World of Warcraft are paradigm cases.

tensions.label: Anti-essentialism vs. the five-element descriptive framework
tensions.claim_a: Family-resemblance refuses necessary-and-sufficient analytic conditions for game-membership (p.8, p.11).
tensions.claim_b: The five-element framework (player / sign / coded rules / sim env props / material medium) appears to identify constitutive components that combine to form games + virtual environments (p.11).
tensions.calleja_resolution: Calleja qualifies the framework as a matrix of components whose configurations VARY across the family — not as a check-list of necessary conditions. The framework is descriptive rather than definitional: it identifies what is being referred to in the rest of the book when central terms are deployed, not what makes something a game tout court.
tensions.residual_pressure: Whether the five-element framework functions in practice as a stealth-essentialism (every virtual game environment HAS all five) is a tension the chapter does not fully discharge. The framework is presented as descriptive but its analytic generality risks operational essentialism.

tensions.label: Experiential-axis primacy vs. object-side description in Ch.1
tensions.claim_a: The book is committed to the experiential axis (p.7).
tensions.claim_b: Ch.1 spends most of its real estate on object-side description — the five elements of the game/virtual environment qua object — before the processual-perspective claim returns at the player-element subsection.
tensions.calleja_resolution: Ch.1 is preparatory-definitional: the descriptive framework is supplied so that subsequent experiential analysis has determinate referents. The processual perspective is registered at every component-description (player as ideal-vs-actual, coded-vs-negotiated rules, computer-vs-player-upheld physics).
tensions.residual_pressure: The chapter's logic depends on the reader holding-in-suspension the object/process distinction; readers who treat the five elements as object-side checklist risk misreading Ch.1 as a structuralism, against the volume's own announced commitment.

tensions.label: Dual-domain performance + actualization claims without phenomenological grounding
tensions.claim_a: Calleja's account of dual-domain performance (p.7) + game-as-process actualization through interaction (p.10) + player-as-active-set-of-practices (p.11) carries strong phenomenological resonance.
tensions.claim_b: No phenomenologist is cited in Ch.1 (Wittgenstein cited only for family-resemblance methodology). Heidegger appears once in the whole volume, in Ch.2 p.21, on tool-disturbance.
tensions.residual_pressure: RESIDUAL-PHENOMENOLOGY-WITHOUT-PHENOMENOLOGIST-CITE FLAG — this is a strong case for the dissertation's anticipatory Aristotelian/Heideggerian grounding layer (Phantasia Cluster + BCAP + Bowin AMT). The actualization-through-interaction motif maps directly onto Aristotelian dunamis/energeia and Heideggerian Vollzug. PROPAGATED PATTERN from IG-03 + IG-10.

game_loci.label: Grand Theft Auto IV (Rockstar North, 2008)
game_loci.calleja_move: Paradigm of digital-games-as-hybrids: GTA IV is better described as a virtual environment containing several embedded games + a linear storyline, with multiple co-present clusters of game-rules. Returns at p.15 in the Wittgensteinian-hybrid-family summary.

game_loci.label: Tetris (Pajitnov, 1985)
game_loci.calleja_move: Tetris-vs-Half-Life-2 contrast deployed to illustrate verbal-disagreement risk in immersion debates.

game_loci.label: Half-Life 2 (Valve Software, 2004)
game_loci.calleja_move: Foil for Tetris in verbal-disagreement example; later cited at p.15 as Wittgensteinian-hybrid + p.16 as paradigm virtual-game-environment for the rest of the book.

game_loci.label: Settlers of Catan (Teuber, 1995)
game_loci.calleja_move: Paradigm for object/process distinction (board + rules + situated activity) and for material-medium specificity (board-game vs. software incarnation).

game_loci.label: Call of Duty IV (Infinity Ward, 2007)
game_loci.calleja_move: Used twice: (a) death-match example for same-object-different-process (player element); (b) hard-coded environmental properties (brick density + bullet penetration + avatar speeds).

game_loci.label: Counter-Strike: Source (Valve Software, 2004)
game_loci.calleja_move: Paradigm for coded + socially-negotiated rule coexistence: clan permitting standard ruleset + locally banning sniper rifles + server-ban enforcement.

game_loci.label: Crysis (Crytek Frankfurt, 2007)
game_loci.calleja_move: High-end of simulated-environmental-properties complexity (alongside CoD: MW2).

game_loci.label: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 (Infinity Ward, 2009)
game_loci.calleja_move: Companion to Crysis at high-end of simulated-environmental-properties complexity.

game_loci.label: World of Warcraft (Blizzard Entertainment, 2004)
game_loci.calleja_move: Paradigm Wittgensteinian-hybrid + virtual-game-environment for the rest of the book; co-paradigm with Half-Life 2.

game_loci.label: Generic non-digital exemplars (poker, fencing, hearts, sudoku, crosswords, tabletop RPG)
game_loci.calleja_move: Poker + fencing invoked at p.8 to illustrate disparate-activity range subsumed under 'game'; tabletop RPG at p.13 for analog simulation of physics; hearts/poker/crosswords/sudoku at p.16 as digitized-but-excluded cases.

interlocutors.label: Ludwig Wittgenstein
interlocutors.role: Methodological anchor for family-resemblance approach to game-definition. The chapter's sole classical-philosophy citation. Used methodologically rather than substantively.

interlocutors.label: Arne Naess
interlocutors.role: Source of 'verbal disagreement' construct — methodological hazard motivating family-resemblance specificity.

interlocutors.label: T. L. Taylor
interlocutors.role: Endorsed processual-view-of-games theorist (alongside Malaby). Returns in IG-03 as methodological forebear.

interlocutors.label: Thomas Malaby
interlocutors.role: Endorsed processual-game-theorist; quoted directly on each-game-as-ongoing-process. Returns in IG-03 against lusory-attitude.

interlocutors.label: Bernard Suits
interlocutors.role: Cited prospectively only — full critique of lusory-attitude deferred to Ch.3. Functions here as the foil against which the processual continuity-with-experience claim is mobilized.

interlocutors.label: Katie Salen + Eric Zimmerman
interlocutors.role: Named as essentialist-foil; charged with adopting Suits's lusory-attitude. The volume's first explicit POSITION-against a Tier-A interlocutor.

interlocutors.label: Jesper Juul
interlocutors.role: Second essentialist-foil; co-named with Salen+Zimmerman as adopting Suits's lusory-attitude. The volume's first explicit POSITION-against a Tier-A interlocutor.

interlocutors.label: Espen Aarseth
interlocutors.role: Source of ergodic-media construct + nontrivial code-to-surface-sign relation. Tier-2 concept import — returns in IG-03 as ergodicity-as-dispositional-readiness.

interlocutors.label: Marie-Laure Ryan
interlocutors.role: Corroborating witness for the digital-games-as-hybrid claim: digital games + tabletop RPGs combine traditional rule-systems with fictional/narrative aspects of predecessor media.

candidate_augmentation_mappings.uexkull_construct: (no direct mapping — family-resemblance is methodological-meta-level, sitting above the Layer C construct catalog)
candidate_augmentation_mappings.rationale: Family-resemblance is a methodological commitment, not a perceptual-action construct. Uexküll-mappings attach to the 5-element FRAMEWORK and to virtual-game-environments below, not to the meta-method.

Every virtual game environment is a designer-constituted Umwelt with bounded perception-action affordances. The Uexküllian Umwelt is arguably more apt than Heideggerian In-der-Welt-sein for the bounded, designer-fabricated nature of these environments. This is the signature payoff of Layer C — and IG-01 is the unit that LICENSES it by declaring 'virtual game environments' as the volume's unit of analysis. PROPAGATED FROM IG-03/IG-10 context: this Umwelt-grounding will return when Calleja's Spatial dimension (IG-05) is mapped to Uexküll's Umwelt and when Incorporation (IG-10) is mapped to the subject's full inhabitation of a designer-fabricated Umwelt.
candidate_augmentation_mappings.provenance: anticipatory-projection (dissertation) — singly anchored, Gibson-bridge falsified per Phase 0 cite-check

candidate_augmentation_mappings.uexkull_construct: Funktionskreis (functional circle): perception-marker (Merkmal) → effect-marker (Wirkmal) → object → perception-marker
candidate_augmentation_mappings.rationale: The five-element framework (player / sign / coded rules / sim env props / material medium) admits a Uexküllian re-reading: PLAYER occupies the subject-pole of the functional circle; REPRESENTATIONAL SIGN bears Merkmal-function (the perception-marker the player reads); CODED RULES + SIMULATED ENVIRONMENTAL PROPERTIES jointly constitute the Wirkmal-system (the effect-marker the world emits and the player acts upon); MATERIAL MEDIUM is the physical-substrate analog of Uexküll's Trägerorganismus + Umweltforschung-equipment.

candidate_augmentation_mappings.layer: Layer B — Burke (1945 Grammar of Motives)
candidate_augmentation_mappings.burke_pentad_mapping: PLAYER ↔ Agent; REPRESENTATIONAL SIGN ↔ Agency (partial); CODED RULES ↔ Agency (rule-as-instrument) + Purpose (rule-as-end); SIMULATED ENVIRONMENTAL PROPERTIES ↔ Scene; MATERIAL MEDIUM ↔ Scene (substrate-level) — Act distributes across PROCESSUAL ENACTMENT itself
candidate_augmentation_mappings.rationale: The five-element framework parallels Burke's pentadic decomposition structurally — both refuse essentialist reduction and instead distribute analytic load across irreducible terms whose ratios (Burke) or configurations (Calleja) vary across cases. Burke is wholly absent from Calleja (Phase 0 cite-check) — mapping is creative-anticipatory, not exegetical.

candidate_augmentation_mappings.layer: Layer A — Aristotle + Heidegger ontological substrate
candidate_augmentation_mappings.ontological_grounding_candidate: Aristotelian dunamis/energeia (potency/actuality) — the dormant code/board pieces/rule set as dunamis, gameplay as energeia. Heideggerian Vollzug (enactment) for the processual side. Phantasia Cluster anchor: Aristotle De Anima III.3 on phantasia as actualization of latent imagery.
candidate_augmentation_mappings.rationale: Calleja's claim that the dormant code, board pieces, or rule set present a potential that is actualized during gameplay is a textbook Aristotelian dunamis/energeia move, made without the Aristotelian vocabulary. This is the RESIDUAL-PHENOMENOLOGY-WITHOUT-PHENOMENOLOGIST-CITE flag of T03 — and arguably the single highest-leverage anticipatory bridge in the chapter.

candidate_augmentation_mappings.ontological_grounding_candidate: Heideggerian Vollzug + Befindlichkeit + verstehen as constitutive of processual enactment; BCAP analyses of being-in-act vs. mere-potency
candidate_augmentation_mappings.rationale: Malaby's claim — quoted approvingly by Calleja — that each game is an ongoing process containing potential for new practices + meanings + refiguration of the game itself parallels Heideggerian Vollzug-ontology. ANTICIPATORY — Heidegger uncited in Ch.1 (single Heidegger appearance in Ch.2 p.21).

candidate_augmentation_mappings.layer: Layer A — Aristotle + Heidegger ontological substrate
candidate_augmentation_mappings.ontological_grounding_candidate: Aristotelian aisthesis (subjective experience domain) + praxis (visible-practice domain) co-presence; Heideggerian Befindlichkeit (mood/attunement) + Rede (visible articulation)
candidate_augmentation_mappings.rationale: Calleja's dual-domain performance claim — that a game's performance occurs in two often-simultaneous domains, the player's subjective experience + the visible practice of playing — is structurally cognate with both the Aristotelian aisthesis-praxis duality and the Heideggerian Befindlichkeit-Rede pair. The dual-domain claim does load-bearing work in licensing the macro/micro temporal-phase distinction of IG-03 (subjective-experience = micro; visible-practice + macro-planning = macro).

candidate_augmentation_mappings.ontological_grounding_candidate: Family-resemblance applied recursively at sub-family-intersection level
candidate_augmentation_mappings.rationale: PROPAGATED FROM IG-03 + IG-10: Calleja's family-resemblance commitment is iterative. At IG-01 it operates on the game-family vs. virtual-environment-family intersection. At IG-03 it returns as the PIM-dimensions-as-overlapping-non-essential-axes. At IG-10 it returns as incorporation-as-family-resemblance-of-experiential-modes. Family-resemblance is the volume's METHODOLOGICAL SIGNATURE, not a local move.
candidate_augmentation_mappings.provenance: exegetical (volume-level methodological pattern verified across IG-01/03/10)
